cse-2003-cs-1.approach: Track what $p$ holds after each iteration: it builds the next Taylor term of $e^x$, and $s$ accumulates those terms.

steps.title: Invariant for p
steps.body:
Initially $p = 1$. In iteration $i$, $p \leftarrow p\cdot\frac{x}{i}$, so after iterations $i = 1, 2, \dots, k$:
$$p = \frac{x}{1}\cdot\frac{x}{2}\cdots\frac{x}{k} = \frac{x^k}{k!}$$

steps.title: Invariant for s
steps.body:
$s$ starts at $1 = \frac{x^0}{0!}$ and each iteration adds the new $p$. The loop runs for $i = 1, \dots, y-1$, so
$$s = \sum_{k=0}^{y-1} \frac{x^k}{k!}$$

steps.title: Large y
steps.body: As $y \to \infty$ this is the Maclaurin series $\sum_{k\ge 0} \frac{x^k}{k!} = e^x$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $x^y$ would need $p$ multiplied by $x$ only; here it is also divided by $i$.
The partial sums $\sum_{k<y} x^k/k!$ converge to $e^x$.
$\ln(1+x)$ has terms $(-1)^{k+1}x^k/k$ — alternating signs and no factorial.
$x^x$ does not depend on the loop structure at all; no such series is formed.

pitfalls: Forgetting that $s$ already includes the $k=0$ term (initial value 1).
